scenes.tts: For twenty years the field insisted sugar broke down through a compound called methylglyoxal, and the theory had an enforcer: Carl Neuberg defended it and also edited the leading biochemical journal.

scenes.tts: In Frankfurt, Gustav Embden kept finding something else. Working under a standard he stated as "meticulous cleanliness and rigorous accuracy," he turned up a three-carbon molecule again and again, and the consensus kept waving it off as contamination. Embden trusted the molecule over the consensus.

scenes.tts: In 1932 he concluded that the phosphoglyceric acid was being converted to pyruvic acid, laid out a unified scheme of glycolysis, and — to get around Neuberg's editorial grip — published it in a clinical journal rather than the biochemical one Neuberg controlled. It was the first correct map of how a cell pulls energy from glucose without oxygen.

scenes.tts: His heart failed in 1933 as the Nazis dismantled his institute and dismissed his Jewish colleagues. Across much of Europe the pathway still bears his name first: Embden–Meyerhof–Parnas.
